What a fee challan has to say

For the office clerk and the accountant About 5 minutes

A fee challan has one job: a parent should be able to read it, believe it, and pay the right amount without ringing the school. Most challans fail at the second step, and almost always for the same two reasons. This is the list we work from.

The eight things it must carry

  1. The child, unambiguously. Name, class and section, and the GR number. Two children with the same name in the same school is not rare, and a challan that cannot tell them apart will eventually be paid against the wrong one.
  2. The month or period it is for. "September 2026", not "this month". A challan found in a drawer in December has to still say what it was for.
  3. Each head as its own line. Tuition, exam, transport, admission. A single total invites the question "what is this for", and answering it on the phone costs more than printing four lines.
  4. Arrears, separately and labelled. Not folded into the tuition line. A parent who sees a tuition figure larger than the one they were told will assume a rise in fees, and they will be right to ask.
  5. Discounts and concessions, shown as a deduction. With a name for the concession. A discount applied by quietly reducing the tuition line is a discount nobody can audit and nobody can renew.
  6. Fines, if any, with what they are for. A late fee with no reason printed beside it is the single most common cause of an argument at the counter.
  7. The amount due and the date it is due by. One figure, in numerals, large. If there is a discounted early-payment amount, both figures with both dates.
  8. A number, and where to pay. A challan number that the office can look up, and the bank or the counter and its hours.

The two that cause almost every dispute

Arrears folded into the current month

A parent owes Rs 3,000 from August and Rs 5,800 for September. If the challan shows one line reading "Tuition Rs 8,800", the parent reads it as a fee increase, comes to the office, and takes twenty minutes of somebody's day. If it shows "September tuition Rs 5,800" and "Arrears, August Rs 3,000", they pay it.

The same rule applies to the arrears total: it should be the sum of named months, not a lump. A parent who disputes an arrears figure is almost never disputing the arithmetic; they are disputing one specific month, and they cannot say which if the challan will not tell them.

Partial payments that the next challan forgets

A parent pays Rs 2,000 against a Rs 5,800 bill in the last week of the month. If the next challan bills the full Rs 5,800 again as arrears, the office has told a paying parent that they did not pay. Worse, they now have a receipt that contradicts the school's own paperwork, and every subsequent conversation starts from there.

A challan that disagrees with a receipt the parent is holding costs more trust than the money involved. Whatever system you use, on paper or on a screen, the test is: does the next challan know about the last payment?

Doing this on paper

It is possible, and plenty of good schools do it. The parts that go wrong are the ones that require cross-referencing rather than writing:

  • Keep one ledger page per family, not per child, and total it. The family is who pays, so the family is the unit that has to balance.
  • Write the receipt number on the ledger line as well as on the receipt. Without it, a dispute six months later has no way back to the original entry.
  • Never erase. Strike through and write the correction beside it with a date and initials. An erased line is indistinguishable from cash that never arrived.
  • Total the day's collection against the receipts before the drawer is closed, not the next morning.

How this works in The School Manager

Every point above is either the default or not optional. Challans carry each head as its own line, arrears are named by month, discounts are recorded against the pupil with an approver and a reason, receipt numbers are issued in an unbroken sequence, and a payment is always known to the next challan because both are entries against the same family rather than two pieces of paper.

The part that is genuinely different from paper is that one payment covers every child in a family at once, and the receipt lists all of them. That is the change a clerk notices in the first week.
